clinicalPearls: A non-progressive anomaly in which iris pigment epithelium extends from the pupillary margin onto the anterior iris surface
It appears as a dark cuff of pigment around the pupil where the posterior pigment layer is visible anteriorly
It is usually unilateral and is a marker of anterior segment maldevelopment
It is strongly associated with glaucoma, which may be present at birth or develop later
Associations include neurofibromatosis type 1, Prader-Willi syndrome and other anterior segment dysgenesis
Lifelong glaucoma surveillance is the key management priority
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital ectropion uveae results from abnormal development of the anterior segment in which the iris posterior pigment epithelium migrates anteriorly over the pupillary margin onto the iris face. It is thought to reflect a neural crest-related developmental abnormality, and the same maldevelopment involves the drainage angle, producing a high-insertion or dysgenic angle that impairs aqueous outflow and causes glaucoma. The pigment ectropion itself is stable, but the associated angle anomaly drives the visually important complication.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired ectropion uveae (from rubeosis or chronic inflammation)
Iris melanoma or other iris lesion (for pigment change)
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination of the pupillary margin and iris
Intraocular pressure measurement and glaucoma assessment
Evaluation for neurofibromatosis type 1 and other associations
Serial monitoring for glaucoma over time
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure or glaucomatous optic neuropathy
Features of neurofibromatosis or another syndrome
New iris changes suggesting an acquired cause
reference.prognosis: The anomaly is stable, and visual prognosis depends on detecting and controlling the associated glaucoma; with effective glaucoma management outcomes can be good.
pitfalls: Failing to screen for and monitor glaucoma
Confusing it with acquired ectropion uveae from neovascularisation
Overlooking neurofibromatosis type 1 and other associations
Assuming a benign course without angle assessment
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Lifelong glaucoma surveillance with regular intraocular pressure measurement, gonioscopy and optic disc assessment is the central priority, as the pigment anomaly itself is stable
Initiate topical pressure-lowering therapy with prostaglandin analogues, beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors or alpha-agonists when glaucoma develops
Proceed to glaucoma surgery such as angle surgery, trabeculectomy or a drainage device when pressure is inadequately controlled medically
Detect and treat amblyopia and correct refractive error, particularly in unilateral paediatric cases
Evaluate for associated conditions including neurofibromatosis type 1 and other anterior segment dysgenesis
Refer to paediatric ophthalmology and glaucoma specialists for coordinated long-term care
